blk_part_01_where_wine_began.text: About 8,000 years ago, farmers in Georgia were already making wine. In 2017, scientists studied pieces of old clay jars from two villages there. The villages, Gadachrili Gora and Shulaveris Gora, are about 50 kilometres south of the capital, Tbilisi. Inside, they found tartaric acid, a chemical that grapes leave behind. It works like a fingerprint of wine. The jars are from about 6000 BC, and they are the oldest sign of grape wine found so far.

blk_part_01_where_wine_began.text: Georgians still make wine in a very old way. They use a qvevri, a large egg-shaped clay jar, buried in the ground up to its neck. They fill it with pressed grapes, together with their skins, stems and seeds. Why bury the jar? The earth keeps the temperature cool and steady, without a fridge. Here, the juice ferments, slowly turning into alcohol. Then the jar is closed, and the wine stays there for months. In 2013, UNESCO added this method to its list of the world's living traditions. Georgians see the marani, the room where the jars are buried, as the holiest place in a family home.

blk_part_02_wine_for_the_pharaohs.text: In 1922, Howard Carter's team opened the tomb, the burial room, of the young king Tutankhamun. Among the treasures were 26 wine jars. Egyptians believed the king would need food and drink in the afterlife, the life after death. The labels on the jars gave the year, the type of wine and its quality. Some also gave the place where the grapes grew and the name of the winemaker. Some of the wine came from the Western River, a branch of the Nile that is desert today. These labels give almost the same information as a wine bottle in a shop now. In 2005 and 2006, scientists tested what was left in the jars. They found both red and white wine.

blk_part_03_wine_and_religion_in_greece_.text: Greek men drank together at a symposium, an evening party with wine, conversation, music and games. It began with a libation: each guest poured a little wine for the gods, mostly for Dionysus. Then a leader, the symposiarch, decided how much water to mix with the wine. They mixed it in a big bowl called a krater, from a Greek word meaning to mix. Many writers describe about three parts water to one part wine. Why add water? The Greeks believed only barbarians, people they saw as wild foreigners, drank pure wine. Mixed wine let guests talk for hours and still think clearly.

blk_part_05_how_monks_and_missionaries_s.text: After the Roman Empire fell, monks, men who live a religious life together, kept wine alive in Europe. The Christian Mass needed wine, so monasteries, the homes of monks, planted vineyards. The Cistercian monks of Cîteaux Abbey in Burgundy, France, created one of the most famous: Clos de Vougeot. Their abbey was founded in 1098. For about 200 years, they bought or were given land. By 1336, they had built a stone wall around it, and the wall still stands. The monks studied their hill closely. They made their best wine from the best soil and simpler wine from the lower parts. This idea, that the place shapes the taste, is still at the heart of Burgundy wine. After the French Revolution of 1789, the monks lost their land. Today more than 80 owners share its 50 hectares.
